title: The Three Weeks, lived
hookLine: many avoid celebrations and haircuts in the weeks before Tisha B'Av
tomorrow: why do people sit on the floor one day a year?

lines: A PEOPLE SITS LIKE A MOURNER.
cards: Midsummer is peak season for weddings, concerts, beach days and fresh haircuts. Right then, some Jews do the opposite: no weddings, no live music, no haircuts. Why would anyone skip haircuts for three weeks?
Because mourners don't cut their hair or throw parties. The weeks run from a fast in the month of Tammuz, remembering Jerusalem's walls breached, to Tisha B'Av, the day of mourning for the Temple.
For a few weeks, a whole people sits a little like a mourner.

teach.h: WHEN AV BEGINS, JOY IS LESSENED.
teach.b: The Mishnah gives the core: when the month of Av begins, joy is lessened. How early the quiet starts is where Jews differ, and each side has a real case.
The Shulchan Aruch, the code of Rabbi Joseph Karo, keeps the strictest customs, like haircuts, to the week of Tisha B'Av itself, a custom kept in Sephardi communities.
Their case: grief kept short stays sharp, and life, weddings included, deserves its room.

teach.h: ASHKENAZI: FROM THE FAST OF TAMMUZ.
teach.b: On the same page, Rabbi Moses Isserles records the Ashkenazi custom of starting from the seventeenth of Tammuz.

Their case: mourning that builds slowly, three weeks, then the nine days, then the day itself, lets you arrive at Tisha B'Av ready to feel it, because nobody switches grief on in an afternoon. Notice what they share.
Both say there's something to grieve. Both lower joy rather than ban life.

And both read the same promise from the prophet Zechariah: "The fast of the fourth month, and the fast of the fifth, and the fast of the seventh, and the fast of the tenth, shall be to the house of Judah joy and gladness, and cheerful seasons."
The quiet weeks point toward a day when they won't be needed.

how: Ashkenazi Jews who keep the Three Weeks generally avoid weddings, live music and haircuts from the seventeenth of Tammuz, with more customs in the nine days; Sephardi custom keeps the strictest practices to the week of Tisha B'Av.

o: seven weeks of counting from Passover to Shavuot
the three pilgrim festivals of the Jewish year
the weeks before Tisha B'Av, kept with lowered joy

games.q: two customs, one season — tap the pairs.
p: when Av begins, joy is lessened

s: Jews all keep the Three Weeks the same way
Ashkenazi custom starts from the seventeenth of Tammuz; Sephardi custom keeps the strictest practices to the final week.
Zechariah promises the summer fasts will become joy
joy and gladness, and cheerful seasons.
during the Three Weeks every kind of joy is forbidden
joy is lowered, not erased; both customs leave room for life.

games.q: your Sephardi friend gets a haircut two weeks before Tisha B'Av, and your Ashkenazi cousin is shocked. give your friend's side its best case.
o: grief kept to the final week stays sharp, and her custom follows the Shulchan Aruch.
she just cares less about the Temple than your cousin does.
haircuts were never part of any Jewish mourning custom.
games.why: both customs are real: Karo's code keeps the strictest customs to the final week; Isserles records the Ashkenazi start from the seventeenth of Tammuz. neither side is the lax one.

practice: Pick one pleasure you could turn down a little for a while: music in the car, a dessert, one more scroll before bed. Name the moment that will tempt you back, and one plan for that moment.
Say the plan to yourself once, plainly, and then let it rest.

wordCard.voice: The Three Weeks: from the fast of Tammuz to Tisha B'Av, a stretch of lowered joy, kept in different ways by different communities.

orig.note: Hebrew: between the narrow straits; a name for the Three Weeks, from Lamentations 1:3.

carryVoice: Something to keep: three quiet weeks, with the joy turned down, never turned off. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mishnah Taanit 4:6 (on the seventeenth of Tammuz the city was breached; when Av enters, joy is lessened)
Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 551:3-4, with the gloss of Rabbi Moses Isserles (Rema) on the Ashkenazi custom from the seventeenth of Tammuz
